titleEn: Do you have money left over?
intro: In this college you'll learn how to talk about money in Dutch: what you spend it on, saving versus spending, amounts in euros, tax words, and how to share your opinion about whether money makes you happy.

paragraphs.heading: Welcome — money, every single day
paragraphs.text: Welcome to theme nineteen. Its title is a real, everyday question: [[Houd je weleens geld over?]], which means 'do you ever have money left over?'. The fuller version you will hear is [[Houd je weleens geld over aan het eind van de maand?]], 'do you ever have money left over at the end of the month?'. Money is something you deal with constantly in the Netherlands — at the supermarket, at the bank, which is the [[de bank]], and when letters arrive in your mailbox. So this is very practical Dutch. Two words sit at the heart of this theme, and they are opposites. The first is [[uitgeven]], which means 'to spend'. The second is [[sparen]], which means 'to save'. A lovely first sentence to learn is [[Ik probeer elke maand wat geld te sparen.]], 'I try to save some money every month'. As always, I explain in English, but every Dutch phrase is spoken by a native Dutch voice, so repeat each one out loud to train your ear and your mouth. Notice the little word [[weleens]] in the title; it simply means 'ever' or 'sometimes', and it makes a question sound gentle and natural. Ready? [[Laten we beginnen!]]

paragraphs.heading: What do you spend money on?
paragraphs.text: Let's learn the most useful pattern of this theme: how to say what you spend money on. In Dutch you use [[geld uitgeven aan]] plus a thing. The verb [[uitgeven]] is what we call a separable verb, so in a normal sentence the little part [[uit]] jumps to the very end. Listen: [[Ik geef veel geld uit aan eten.]], 'I spend a lot of money on food'. Or the opposite: [[Wij geven weinig geld uit aan kleding.]], 'we spend little money on clothes'. To ask a friend, you say [[Waar geef jij je geld aan uit?]], 'what do you spend your money on?'. A common confession is [[Hij geeft te veel geld uit aan spelletjes.]], 'he spends too much money on games'. Now remember the opposite verb, [[sparen]]. You might say [[Ik geef minder uit en ik spaar meer.]], 'I spend less and I save more'. Many people put money aside in a savings account, which is [[de spaarrekening]]. A practical question to ask someone is [[Waar geef jij het meeste geld aan uit?]], 'what do you spend the most money on?'. Try answering that about your own life right now, out loud, using [[Ik geef het meeste geld uit aan]] and then your answer.

paragraphs.heading: Euros, amounts and 'too much'
paragraphs.text: Now let's handle amounts of money, because you need them every day. The currency is the euro, [[de euro]], and the cents are [[de cent]]. A price like three euros fifty is spoken [[drie euro vijftig]]. Bigger amounts are useful too: a hundred is [[honderd]], two hundred and fifty is [[tweehonderdvijftig]], and a thousand is [[duizend]]. So a rent might be [[De huur is achthonderd euro per maand.]], 'the rent is eight hundred euros per month'. The word for rent is [[de huur]], and your salary is [[het salaris]]. Here is a small but crucial word: [[te]], which means 'too' in the sense of 'more than you want'. So [[te duur]] means 'too expensive' and [[te goedkoop]] means 'too cheap'. Listen: [[Die jas is te duur, ik koop hem niet.]], 'that coat is too expensive, I'm not buying it'. You also have [[te veel]], 'too much', and [[te weinig]], 'too little'. A very honest sentence for the end of the month is [[Ik heb deze maand te weinig geld over.]], 'this month I have too little money left over'. Be careful not to confuse [[te duur]] with [[heel duur]]: the second just means 'very expensive', a simple fact, while [[te duur]] means it is a problem for you.

paragraphs.heading: Bills, tax and the Belastingdienst
paragraphs.text: Letters about money arrive often in the Netherlands, so let's build your tax and bill vocabulary. A bill is [[de rekening]], the amount on it is [[het bedrag]], and tax is [[de belasting]]. The tax office is called the [[Belastingdienst]], and it sends you a [[belastingaanslag]] — that is the official letter telling you how much tax you must pay, or how much you get back. Two very practical sentences: [[Ik heb een belastingaanslag ontvangen.]], 'I have received a tax assessment', and the hopeful question [[Krijg ik geld terug van de belasting?]], 'will I get money back from the tax office?'. When you phone an organisation, always use the polite form [[u]] and polite openers. For example [[Kunt u mij uitleggen waarom dit bedrag zo hoog is?]], 'can you explain to me why this amount is so high?'. To check a bill you ask [[Klopt dit bedrag wel?]], 'is this amount actually correct?'. If money is tight, this sentence is gold: [[Mag ik in termijnen betalen?]], 'may I pay in instalments?'. One cultural tip: the Netherlands has support payments called [[toeslagen]], such as rent or healthcare allowance, the [[de toeslag]]. If you have a low income, you may be able to apply for one, so it is well worth asking about.

paragraphs.heading: Does money make you happy? Your opinion
paragraphs.text: This theme also invites you to give your opinion, which is a wonderful A2 skill. The key building block is [[Ik vind dat]], which means 'I think that' or 'in my opinion'. After it, you give a whole little sentence. For example [[Ik vind dat geld niet het belangrijkste is.]], 'I think money is not the most important thing'. A famous idea in Dutch is [[Geld maakt niet altijd gelukkig.]], 'money does not always make you happy'. You can agree by saying [[Dat klopt]], 'that's true', or [[Ik ben het ermee eens]], 'I agree'. To disagree gently you say [[Ik ben het er niet mee eens]], 'I don't agree'. To add a reason, use the word [[omdat]], 'because': [[Ik vind dat geld belangrijk is, omdat ik mijn rekeningen moet betalen.]], 'I think money is important, because I have to pay my bills'. There are great Dutch sayings here too. People say [[Geld groeit niet aan de bomen.]], 'money doesn't grow on trees', meaning you must work for it. And a thrifty person says [[Ik moet op de kleintjes letten.]], 'I have to watch the pennies'. Try finishing this sentence yourself, out loud: [[Ik vind dat]] and then your own honest opinion about money.

paragraphs.heading: A real moment — and well done
paragraphs.text: Let's put it all together in a real situation. Imagine a letter arrives and the amount looks wrong, so you phone the tax office. You hear [[Belastingdienst, goedemorgen. Waarmee kan ik u helpen?]], 'tax office, good morning, how can I help you?'. You answer politely: [[Goedemorgen. Ik heb een belastingaanslag gekregen, maar ik begrijp het bedrag niet.]], 'good morning, I have received a tax assessment, but I don't understand the amount'. They check, and say you must pay three hundred euros, [[U moet driehonderd euro betalen.]]. That feels like a lot, so you ask [[Mag ik in termijnen betalen?]], 'may I pay in instalments?', and they reply [[Ja, dat kan.]], 'yes, that's possible'. You close warmly with [[Dank u wel voor uw hulp.]], 'thank you very much for your help'. See how far you have come? You can talk about spending and saving, say amounts in euros, handle a bill or a [[belastingaanslag]], and share your opinion. Money talk is intimidating in any language, so be proud. Practise one phrase from today out loud, and remember: [[Geld maakt niet altijd gelukkig.]] [[Heel goed gedaan!]] Well done — and I'll see you in the next theme!
